entry: American actress and dancer. Orphaned at four, she became a Ziegfeld girl and then a Broadway star before moving to films in 1929. Directors including [[Frank Capra]], [[Cecil B. DeMille]] and [[Fritz Lang]] favored her, and she made 86 films in 38 years before turning to television. She was nominated for four [[Academy Awards]] and won three Primetime Emmy Awards, including for the [[Western (genre)|Western]] series *The Big Valley*.

Lion population of the [[Maghreb]] in North Africa, extinct in the wild. Also called the Atlas lion, it was a population of *Panthera leo leo* that ranged from [[Morocco]] to Egypt. The spread of [[Firearm|firearms]] and bounties for shooting lions eradicated it, though small groups may have survived in [[Algeria]] until the early 1960s and in Morocco until the mid-1960s. Fossils between 100,000 and 110,000 years old were found in the Bizmoune cave near Essaouira. Until 2017 it was considered a distinct subspecies, but genetic and morphological analyses showed it does not differ significantly from the [[Asiatic lion]].

[[Fashion]] doll franchise made by the American toy company Mattel. Businesswoman Ruth Handler, who co-founded Mattel with her husband Elliot, based the doll on the German Bild Lilli doll she had bought while in Europe. Introduced on March 9, 1959, at the American International Toy Fair in [[New York City]], Barbie was marketed as a teenage fashion model, and her clothing line was designed to drive ongoing sales. Mattel has sold over a billion Barbie dolls, and since 1984 the brand has expanded into video games, animated films and television series.

Critics argue that Barbie's slim figure and accessories promoted unattainable ideals of thinness, and in 2016 Mattel introduced dolls with varied body types.

Class of depressant drugs derived from barbituric acid. Barbiturates were long used as anxiolytics and hypnotics and are still used as anticonvulsants, but they carry risks of addiction and overdose and are controlled in most countries. [[Benzodiazepine|Benzodiazepines]] have largely replaced them in routine medical practice because of their lower overdose risk. Barbiturates are still used in general [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]], for [[Epilepsy|epilepsy]] and [[Migraine|acute migraines]], and in [[Euthanasia]] and capital punishment by [[Lethal injection]].

American singer, songwriter and actress. She began performing in the early 1960s and signed with [[Columbia Records]], retaining full artistic control of her performances in exchange for lower pay. She was the first woman to score 11 number one albums on the U.S. Billboard 200, and remains the only artist to top the chart in six decades. She won an [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actress in *Funny Girl* (1968), and with *Yentl* (1983) became the first woman to write, produce, direct and star in a major studio film. She has earned all four major performing arts awards: Emmy, Grammy, Oscar and Tony.

Capital and largest city of [[Catalonia]], on the northeastern coast of Spain (pop., 2025: 1,732,066). It is the second-most populous municipality in Spain after [[Madrid]] and lies on the [[Mediterranean Sea]] between the Llobregat and Besòs rivers. The Roman colony of Barcino was founded on the site. In the Middle Ages Barcelona became capital of the County of Barcelona and, after the dynastic union with the [[Kingdom of Aragon]], the most important city in the Crown of Aragon. It was capital of autonomous Catalonia from 1931, and was under French control briefly during the 17th-century Reapers' War and again from 1812 to 1814 under [[Napoleon]].

The architectural works of [[Antoni Gaudí]] and Lluís Domènech i Montaner are [[UNESCO]] World Heritage Sites. Barcelona hosted the 1992 Summer Olympics. Its port is one of Europe's principal seaports, and [[FC Barcelona]] is the city's football club.

Optical, machine-readable representation of data.

Linear barcodes encode data in parallel lines whose widths, spacings and sizes vary, and are read by optical scanners. Later two-dimensional (2D) matrix codes use rectangles, dots or hexagons, and can be read by a digital camera running software, such as on a [[Smartphone|smartphone]]. The barcode was based on [[Morse code]] extended to thin and thick bars, and was patented in the U.S. in 1952 by Norman Joseph Woodland and Bernard Silver. Their first working system used [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] ink, which faded.

Barcodes became commercially successful after they were adopted to automate supermarket checkout. In 1973 the Uniform Grocery Product Code Council chose a vertical-bar design by George Laurer. The U.K. supermarket group Sainsbury's used one of the first successful systems in 1972, and in June 1974 a Marsh supermarket in Troy, Ohio, scanned a Universal Product Code on a pack of Wrigley's chewing gum. [[QR code|QR codes]], a 2D type, rose in popularity in the second decade of the 2000s with growing smartphone ownership.

Marginal sea of the [[Arctic Ocean]], off northern Norway and Russia. Shallow, with an average depth of 230 meters (750 ft), it covers about 1.4 million sq km and is important for fishing and hydrocarbon exploration. The sea is named after the Dutch navigator [[Willem Barentsz]], who explored its waters. Its southern half remains ice-free year-round because of the warm North Atlantic drift. It is bordered by the Kola Peninsula, [[Svalbard]] and [[Novaya Zemlya]], whose islands separate it from the [[Kara Sea]]. Warming has reduced sea ice, and the sea has been described as "turning into the Atlantic." A 2010 treaty between Norway and Russia settled a long-standing maritime boundary dispute.

Flat-bottomed boat without its own means of mechanical propulsion. Barges were originally used on inland waterways and are now used on both inland and marine waters. Modern barges are pulled by tugs or pushed by pusher boats. In Great Britain the merchant barge was a flat-bottomed vessel for navigable rivers, often with sails. During the [[Industrial Revolution]], a network of canals was built in [[United Kingdom|Great Britain]] from 1750 onward, and the narrowboat was developed to give full access to it. Today barges include hopper barges for dry bulk cargo, tank barges for liquids and deck barges for oversized goods. The U.S. inland barge fleet moves about 630 million tons of cargo annually across 12,000 miles of waterways.

Port and university city, capital of [[Apulia]] on the [[Adriatic Sea]] in southern Italy. Its population is 316,248, and the metropolitan city, Italy's fifth-largest, has 1,218,073 people. In antiquity it was a Greek-influenced harbor, and it became part of the [[Roman Republic]] in the 3rd century BC. The arrival of the relics of [[Saint Nicholas]] in 1087 made it a major pilgrimage site. The old town contains the Basilica of Saint Nicholas, the Cathedral of San Sabino and the Norman-Swabian Castle, while the Murat quarter to the south is the modern center, laid out on a grid.

Group of surgical procedures used to manage [[Obesity|obesity]] and related conditions. Also called metabolic surgery, these operations produce weight loss by altering gut [[Hormone|hormones]], reducing stomach size or reducing nutrient absorption. Standard procedures include Roux-en-Y bypass, sleeve gastrectomy and biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch. In morbidly obese people it is the most effective treatment for weight loss and for reducing complications. A 2021 meta-analysis associated it with reduced all-cause mortality among obese adults with or without type 2 diabetes.

Chemical element with symbol Ba and atomic number 56.

A soft, silvery [[Alkaline earth metal|alkaline earth metal]] in group 2, barium is never found free in nature because of its high reactivity. Its most common minerals are barite (barium sulfate) and witherite (barium carbonate). The name comes from the Greek *barys*, meaning "heavy." Barium was identified in 1772 and first reduced to a metal in 1808 by [[Humphry Davy]] through [[Electrolysis|electrolysis]]. Barium compounds color [[Fireworks|fireworks]] green, and barium sulfate is added to [[Oil well|oil well]] drilling fluid and used as an X-ray contrast agent for imaging the gastrointestinal tract. Soluble barium compounds are poisonous and have been used as rodenticides.

Outermost layers of the stems and roots of woody plants.

Bark refers to all tissues outside the [[Vascular cambium|vascular cambium]] and consists of inner bark and outer bark. In older stems the inner bark is living tissue, while the outer bark includes dead surface tissue and is also called the rhytidome. Bark is found only on woody plants; herbaceous plants and young stems lack it. Cork, derived from the cork cambium, is the outermost layer and protects the plant from parasites, herbivores, disease, dehydration and fire.

Products derived from bark include [[Tannin|tannin]], [[Resin|resin]], cork and spices, and bark has been used to make cloth, canoes and [[Rope|ropes]]. Removing bark is called decortication.

Cereal grain, *Hordeum vulgare*, a member of the grass family. Barley was among the first grains domesticated, in the [[Fertile Crescent]] around 9000 BC, and its use had spread across [[Eurasia]] by 2000 BC. It grows best in relatively low temperatures and well-drained soil, and tolerates drought and soil salinity, but is less winter-hardy than [[Wheat|wheat]] or rye. In 2023 barley was the fourth most produced grain, at 146 million tonnes, behind [[Maize|maize]], [[Rice|rice]] and wheat. About 70% of production goes to animal feed and about 30% to beer, whisky and foods. It is also used in soups, stews and barley [[Bread|bread]], and in English folklore John Barleycorn personifies the grain.

Agricultural building used for storage and as a covered workplace.

In North America a barn houses [[Livestock|livestock]], equipment, fodder and often grain, and is usually qualified by use, as in [[Dairy|dairy]] barn or tobacco barn. In the British Isles and Europe the term is mainly used for storage of unthreshed cereals and fodder, while cow shelters are called byres and horses are kept in [[Stable|stables]]. The word comes from Old English bere-aern, meaning storehouse for barley. The modern barn developed from the medieval tithe barn, and by the 15th century several thousands of these barns stood in Western Europe. In the late 19th century barns added [[Silo|silos]] for silage preservation, and in the 20th century electricity and tractors reduced manual labor.

Sessile marine [[Crustacean|crustacean]] of the subclass Cirripedia.

Some 2,100 species have been described. Most adults are attached to a surface and filter-feed on plankton using long, feathery cirri. Acorn barnacles are fixed by cement glands and grow hard calcareous shells. Barnacles are related to [[Crab|crabs]] and [[Lobster|lobsters]] and have existed since at least the mid-[[Carboniferous]], some 325 million years ago. As biofouling on ships they cause [[Drag (physics)|hydrodynamic drag]], reducing efficiency.

[[Red dwarf]] star in the constellation [[Ophiuchus]].

At 5.96 light-years away, it is the fourth-nearest known individual star to the Sun, after the three components of [[Alpha Centauri]], and the closest star in the northern celestial hemisphere. In 1916 Edward Emerson Barnard measured its proper motion at 10.3 arcseconds per year, the highest known for any star. Four sub-Earth-mass planets orbit it, discovered by two independent teams of astronomers in 2024–2025.

American children's television series starring Barney the Dinosaur. Created by Sheryl Leach, the preschool series featured an anthropomorphic purple Tyrannosaurus rex who conveyed educational messages through songs and dances. It aired on [[PBS]] from April 6, 1992, to November 2, 2010, and was the flagship of the Barney franchise. Its popularity with children drew severe criticism from adults, who parodied it in comedy routines, including one on [[Saturday Night Live]], and the U.S. Army used its music to psychologically torture and interrogate Iraqi prisoners of war.

Scientific instrument for measuring atmospheric pressure.

Pressure tendency derived from barometric readings can forecast short-term changes in the weather, and pressure measurements help locate troughs, pressure systems and frontal boundaries on surface weather analysis. A pressure altimeter is essentially the same instrument, calibrated to estimate altitude. Average sea-level pressure is 1013 hPa (mbar). Evangelista Torricelli is usually credited with inventing the [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] barometer in 1643, though historian W. E. Knowles Middleton suggests 1644. The aneroid barometer, invented in 1843 by Lucien Vidie, uses an evacuated metal capsule instead of liquid.

Western style of architecture, music, dance, painting and other arts, c. 1600–1750.

The style flourished from the early 1600s until the 1750s, following Renaissance art and [[Mannerism]]. It was encouraged by the [[Catholic Church]] to counter the austerity of Protestant art and architecture, and it used contrast, movement, exuberant detail and grandeur to inspire awe. It began in Rome and spread to Italy, France, Spain, [[Portugal]], Austria and Russia. In the 1730s it evolved into the more flamboyant [[Rococo]]. The word derives from the Portuguese term for an irregularly shaped pearl, and in the 18th century it began to be used unflatteringly for music.

Highly decorative and theatrical European architectural style, 16th–18th century.

It appeared in Italy in the late 16th century and was introduced by the [[Catholic Church]], particularly the Jesuits, to counter the Reformation with buildings meant to inspire astonishment and awe. Architects made Renaissance elements such as domes and colonnades higher, grander and more dramatic, and used painted ceilings to suggest looking up into heaven. The High Baroque (1625–1675) peaked in Italy, Spain, Portugal, France, Bavaria and Austria. [[Gian Lorenzo Bernini|Bernini]] designed the colonnade of St. Peter's Square, and the Hall of Mirrors at the [[Palace of Versailles]] reflects the more ordered Late Baroque in France under [[Louis XIV]]. About 1730 the ornate [[Rococo]] variant appeared in Central Europe.

Style of Western classical music from about 1600 to 1750.

It followed the Renaissance and was followed by the [[Classical period (music)|Classical period]] after a short transition. The period formalized common-practice tonality and established the mixed vocal and instrumental forms of [[Opera|opera]], cantata and oratorio, as well as the solo [[Concerto|concerto]] and sonata. [[Claudio Monteverdi]] was an early opera pioneer, and [[Antonio Vivaldi]] composed over 500 concertos. [[Johann Sebastian Bach]], [[George Frideric Handel|Handel]] and [[Henry Purcell]] were also central. Performances were typically accompanied by a basso continuo group, and musicians were expected to improvise.

Large, predatory, ray-finned saltwater [[Fish|fish]] of the genus *Sphyraena*.

Barracudas, the only genus in the family Sphyraenidae, have elongated bodies and sharp, fang-like teeth set in large jaws. They are found in tropical and subtropical oceans worldwide, from the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] to the [[Red Sea]] and the [[Caribbean Sea]], usually near the surface and around coral reefs and sea grasses. The genus contains 26 species. The great barracuda, *Sphyraena barracuda*, grows over 1.5 m long and can reach 58 km/h in pursuit. Barracudas are often targeted by sport-fishing enthusiasts, and their flesh can carry toxins that cause ciguatera fish poisoning.

Catadromous [[Fish|fish]], *Lates calcarifer*, of the Indo-West Pacific, also called Asian sea bass. Its name, from an Aboriginal language of [[Queensland]], means "large-scaled river fish." Adults inhabit coastal waters and estuaries, while juveniles live in freshwater. At the start of the [[Monsoon|monsoon]], males migrate downriver to meet females, which lay several million eggs each. The fish is farmed in [[Aquaculture|aquaculture]] across Southeast Asia and Australia, and is also prized as a gamefish.

Spiral galaxy with a central bar-shaped structure composed of stars.

About two-thirds of spiral galaxies in the local universe are barred, and the [[Milky Way]] is one. [[Edwin Hubble|Hubble]] classified them as "SB" in his sequence, with subtypes from SBa, which have tightly bound arms, to SBc, which have loosely bound arms; SB0 is a barred [[Lenticular galaxy|lenticular galaxy]]. The bar channels gas inward, fueling [[Star formation|star formation]] near the center, and many barred spirals have active galactic nuclei. Bars are thought to be temporary, decaying over time into more regular spirals. A 2008 investigation found that 20% of spiral galaxies in the distant past had bars, compared with about 65% of local ones.
